description:
Looking for an UI expert to make a working prototype more exciting and fun. Also anyone who likes to dive deeper into the sphereX data and api capabilities is welcome. Are you interested in Astrophysics and have a knack for AI or data analytics? Join the team. Let's look for more events in the data and how to create a stellar screen design visualizing our changing universe.
I have created a web application that navigates the data and visualizes some events.
summary: SPHEREx Time Scan is a public web tool for NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey. Enter coordinates, a sexagesimal position or an object name and it finds every SPHEREx visit covering that patch of sky, then plays them as a short film you can scrub, blink or subtract — so anything that moved or changed between visits stands out immediately. It reads the public IRSA archive live, with no API keys and nothing to download, includes the five objects named in the challenge as presets, overlays Gaia DR3 and AllWISE, summarises the mission's contamination FLAGS and ranks "what changed here?" candidates. Built with FastAPI, React/TypeScript and astropy; 205 offline tests.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx photographs the whole sky roughly every six months in 102 near-infrared bands — over a billion objects, about four visits per field. SPHEREx Time Scan turns that archive into something a person can actually look at. Enter a position (decimal degrees, sexagesimal such as 08h55m10.831s −7d14m42.53s, or an object name) and the tool asks the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive which SPHEREx exposures cover that patch of sky, then shows every visit of that field in any detector band.

From there: scrub the visits frame by frame, or press play and watch them as a short film at 1–8 fps (spacebar, loop, next frame prefetched); blink two epochs; subtract one epoch from another with automatic registration — visits from different seasons differ in roll by about 180°, so the difference is registered onto a common frame and reports how much was rotated; plot a light curve of the median surface brightness per visit; and run a "what changed here?" queue that ranks sources which do not persist across visits. Gaia DR3 and AllWISE are overlaid with proper motions projected to each exposure's epoch, the mission's own FLAGS bits are summarised for the crop on screen, and a WCS ring (or an off-frame arrow) marks the target. Every view is a URL, so any frame can be handed to someone else as a link.

The five objects named in the challenge — Barnard's Star, ε Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis — are curated presets with real SPHEREx visits; the two variables open directly in Difference, where the brightness change is what you can actually see.

How it works

The backend (Python, FastAPI, astropy, numpy, Pillow) queries IRSA TAP/ADQL for the exposures covering a position, then reads only the rows of each FITS cube that contain the crop over HTTP range reads — about 1 MB instead of a 66 MB file — and renders a PNG. Cutouts, epoch lists, FLAGS summaries and catalogue cross-matches are cached on disk and shared between visitors, with bounded size and a fallback index snapshot so the app keeps working when the archive is slow or down. The frontend is React + TypeScript + Vite, canvas-rendered, with a typed API client and URL-state routing. 205 backend tests run fully offline against fixtures.

Why it matters

The bottleneck in time-domain astronomy is not the data, it is the vetting: someone has to look at each patch of sky more than once and decide whether a source moved or changed. SPHEREx makes that comparison possible for the whole sky and impossible to do by hand. This tool reduces it to two clicks for a student, a teacher or a journalist — no account, no download, no API key, no astronomy software.

Tools and data

Python 3.13, FastAPI, uvicorn, astropy, numpy, Pillow, pytest; React 18, TypeScript, Vite; NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx quick-release images, TAP, WISE/AllWISE), JPL Horizons, ESA Gaia DR3, CDS SIMBAD/SESAME, GitHub.

Considerations

No credentials and no pre-downloaded dataset: everything is read live from public archives, so a new SPHEREx release is picked up without a code change. The limits are stated in the app rather than hidden — 6.2″ per pixel, a ~7.5″ PSF, a 5σ depth around 230 µJy (AB 18) measured from a real variance extension — and the app says what it can and cannot see. The disk cache is bounded, archive outages fall back to a local index snapshot, and there is no claim of a discovery: candidates are ranked, not announced.

Super Intelligence use

AI assistants were used for research, code review, debugging and drafting documentation. All code was reviewed, tested and run by the team; no AI-generated NASA branding, logos or mission identifiers were used.
